original_question: Let f be a nonzero function in L1(R), and let Lambda be a nonempty discrete subset of R with bounded density, meaning that sup_x #(Lambda intersect [x, x+1)) < +infinity. Assume that f + Lambda tiles R at level zero. Must Lambda have a uniform density D(Lambda), in the sense that #(Lambda intersect [x, x+r)) = D(Lambda) * r + o(r) as r -> +infinity uniformly in x? Equivalently, if a nonempty bounded-density set Lambda has the Fourier transform of its point-mass measure delta_Lambda vanishing on some open interval, does that force Lambda to have a uniform density?
target_in_paper: Section 6.1, the unnumbered open problem on tilings at level zero, already foreshadowed in Section 1.2 immediately after Theorem 1.3.
correct_elements: Your draft is very close to the paper’s exact open problem. It correctly uses the one-dimensional setting ℝ, assumes f ∈ L^1(ℝ) is nonzero, takes Λ ⊂ ℝ to be nonempty, discrete, and of bounded density, asks about level-zero tilings, and states the paper’s notion of uniform density with the error term uniform in x. It also matches the paper’s explicit Fourier-analytic reformulation using the point-mass measure δ_Λ and the vanishing of its Fourier transform on an open interval. Just as in the paper, your question is narrowly about whether bounded-density level-zero tilings force uniform density, not about periodicity or zero integral.
missing_details: The paper’s tiling hypothesis means explicitly that ∑_{λ∈Λ} f(x−λ) = 0 for almost every x, and that this series converges absolutely almost everywhere; this should be stated if the question is to be fully stand-alone (Section 1, equation (1.1), p. 1).

The paper defines bounded density by sup_{x∈ℝ} #(Λ ∩ [x, x+1)) < ∞ and uniform density by #(Λ ∩ [x, x+r)) = D(Λ)·r + o(r) as r → ∞ uniformly in x; these exact half-open intervals are part of the official formulation (Section 1.1, equations (1.2) and (1.3), p. 2).

In the Fourier-analytic version, one should define δ_Λ := ∑_{λ∈Λ} δ_λ and understand its Fourier transform in the tempered-distribution sense; bounded density is what guarantees δ_Λ is a tempered distribution (Section 2.1, equation (2.2) and surrounding text, pp. 5-6).
The paper’s equivalent reformulation says that ^hδ_Λ vanishes on some open interval (a,b); it is not required that this interval be centered at 0 (Section 6.1, pp. 19-20).

The paper already proves in Theorem 1.3 that under the level-zero tiling assumptions Λ must be relatively dense, so if a uniform density exists then it is automatically strictly positive; this is nearby context worth making explicit (Section 1.2, Theorem 1.3 and Section 6.1, pp. 2 and 20).
A paper-faithful formulation should mention that this is an open problem, not a theorem or conjecture proved in the paper (Section 6.1, pp. 19-20).
refined_question: Let f ∈ L^1(ℝ) be nonzero, and let Λ ⊂ ℝ be a nonempty discrete set of bounded density, meaning that sup_{x∈ℝ} #(Λ ∩ [x, x+1)) < ∞. Assume that f + Λ is a tiling of ℝ at level 0, i.e. ∑_{λ∈Λ} f(x−λ) = 0 for almost every x and the series converges absolutely almost everywhere. Must Λ have a uniform density? Equivalently, must there exist D(Λ) such that #(Λ ∩ [x, x+r)) = D(Λ)·r + o(r) as r → ∞ uniformly in x?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, let Λ ⊂ ℝ be nonempty and of bounded density, and let δ_Λ := ∑_{λ∈Λ} δ_λ. If the Fourier transform ^hδ_Λ vanishes on some open interval (a,b), does it follow that Λ has a uniform density?
justification: The draft is targeting the exact open problem stated in Section 6.1 rather than a neighboring theorem. Section 1.2 first asks, immediately after Theorem 1.3, whether the hypotheses of Theorem 1.3 force Λ to have a uniform density, and Section 6.1 repeats that question as an open problem and then gives the Fourier-analytic equivalent formulation. To make the question fully stand-alone and paper-faithful, one must include the formal tiling definition from equation (1.1), the exact definitions of bounded density and uniform density from equations (1.2)-(1.3), and the distributional meaning of δ_Λ and ^hδ_Λ from Section 2.1. The nearby context also matters: Theorem 1.3 shows that Λ is at least relatively dense, while Lemma 3.2 explains a special case where uniform density is known if ^hδ_Λ agrees with cδ_0 near 0; Section 6.1 explicitly says the open problem is nontrivial because that special situation need not occur.
